text: The arrangement runs on checks: an older, rich man pays, a college student keeps her place in the lecture hall, and nothing else passes between them. Walter Reisch made this in 1935 and set it thirteen years earlier, in a Vienna where one sudden financial disaster is enough to reorganize a young woman's life without anyone behaving badly. The comedy is not farce. It lives in the gap between what an arrangement is and what it looks like from a doorway, and it takes its time, a hundred and five minutes for a premise that fits in a sentence. Then the tutor of the rich man's sons falls into it, carrying the reading almost anyone would make, and the film settles down to work with a fact it cannot get around: the truth here is duller than the rumor, and much harder to say out loud.

David Trueman finishes his training and goes to Bolivia to practice medicine among people nobody is counting. What he finds there is corruption and force, neither of which has any argument with him; they simply outlast his intentions, and he drifts from the clinic into the drug trade and then out of the country. Ian Pringle's film is an Australian production that spends none of its ninety-seven minutes in Australia, and the trouble it describes is not local to anywhere. Its one listed honor is for cinematography, which sets a fair expectation: what happens to this man will be visible before it is ever stated. In the United States he meets Mary, who is using heroin and who understands, without being told, what he has come away from. Two people at a low ebb, talking. The film is patient with that.

Somebody behind the Belgian lines has been handed morale as a task, the way another man is handed a supply count. That is Francis's assignment in Lukas Dhont's film, and it puts him in the path of Pierre, a young soldier who came to this war wanting to be seen doing well in it. Two hours, in French, on the near side of the front: not the trench picture the label promises but the zone just behind it, where an army administers its own feelings and the fighting arrives at one remove. Pierre wants a witness to his courage. Francis needs a method for producing other men's. Those are not the same want, and the interest lies in how long two people can go on treating them as though they were.

Half the film never leaves the ship, and the water the ship is crossing is not safe. Marcel L'Herbier fills a French vessel with passengers in wartime, gives it a secret mission they know nothing about, and lets Jeanne — who once loved the first officer and now finds him unaccountably preoccupied — do the noticing. Veille d'armes runs eighty minutes and keeps two machines going at once: an espionage plot that withholds its own logic for as long as it can, and a romance fastened to the outside of it. The first explains why the officers behave strangely. The second explains why anyone aboard would take that behavior personally. Made two decades after the war it depicts, it is most alert to the ordinary people carried along inside a decision nobody has told them about.

The police have their man; what they lack is a confession, so they set about producing one. A girl of eight was killed in 1927 in the countryside outside Berlin, and the suspect is a Polish guest worker, which in the eyes of the men questioning him is most of what he is. Ottokar Runze made it in 1976 and made it as docudrama, ninety-two minutes, and the form settles what kind of interest the film can hold: not the crime, but what a room and a set of questions can be brought to yield. The method is the subject. Tension here is not mystery but duration — the length of time a man can keep saying no to a question that keeps changing shape, and the length of time the men across the table are willing to keep asking it.

Her father defended members of Narodnaya Volya in court, which is one way of saying Vera Protasova came to her politics by inheritance before she came to them by choice. The film puts her among the first people around the Social Democratic Party in Russia at the start of the century, when it was still mostly conversation, travel and risk. Ninety-two minutes, made in the Soviet Union in 1986, which puts unusual weight on a story about early meetings and early loyalties. What keeps working is the household she comes from. A lawyer's daughter, raised in rooms where the law was a profession and the accused were clients, walks out to join the people the law had been written against. Comfort is what she has to spend, and the film counts it.

A soldier arrives at a secluded Protestant village in the middle of the Thirty Years' War and announces that the long-abandoned manor there belongs to him. The claim is the least false thing about him. Markus Schleinzer gives this ninety-three minutes and a lead performance that took a Silver Bear, the right honor for a film in which nearly every exchange is also an audition: name, rank, faith, and the person underneath all three, offered up for acceptance by neighbors with long memories about who belongs. What Rose wants is recognition, which is the one thing that cannot be seized. It has to be granted, again and again, by people who could stop granting it any morning. For a story set in a war, that makes an odd engine — the danger sits at the level of manners.

Revenge in this one runs downhill: the head of the organization first, then everyone under him, in order. The list is the plot. The man working it kills for money by trade, and the outfit he is taking apart is the one he holds responsible for his mother's death, which gives the ninety minutes the rhythm of a job rather than a quest — the next scene is always known, and the only open question is what it costs to reach it. Released as El enviado de la muerte, the film puts its weight on one exact distinction: between killing for a fee, which is work and has an end to it, and killing on his own account, which nobody is paying for and no name crossed off the list will settle.

News gets out that the parish priest has been offered a cardinal's position, and the mountain village promptly rearranges itself around him. The offer comes from his nephew, who happens to be the emperor. The priest is Napoleon's uncle. Everyone who comes calling afterward is less interested in congratulating him than in working out what a cardinal in the family might be worth to them. Flavio Calzavara made it in 1941 and kept it to eighty-three minutes, about the length of an anecdote told well. The comedy is in the mismatch of scale: an empire's notion of a favor lands in a place where a favor means one specific thing done for one specific person, and everybody who wants one has to ask a man they see every Sunday.

The crew rents a room from a woman who notices things, and their cover story is that they are a band. That decision does more work than the robbery does: it obliges a group of men with nothing in common to sustain a fiction indoors, at close quarters, under a landlady who is sharp, present, and not going anywhere. A heist that has to be run past a landlady is a heist with house rules. Ethan Coen's film runs a hundred and four minutes on Southern courtesy stretched well past the point where courtesy can bear the load. The professor at the center is eccentric first and charming second, and the design lets charm keep working until it meets the one person it cannot move. A casino sits at the far end of the plan. Almost nothing that matters happens there.

Robbie has just missed a prison sentence and become a father, in that order, and neither fact opens a door. Then there is a visit to a distillery. Ken Loach's film starts in the vocabulary of the court — conditions, terms, the machinery that decides what a young man with a record may do next — and finds a second vocabulary in casks and years and a trade that rewards a nose rather than a certificate. That turn is the joke and also the case the film is making: skill is one of the few valuable things nobody can confiscate. A hundred and one minutes, and the award it carries went to its composer, which says something about where the tone ends up. Robbie and his mates are not being studied here. They are being handed something to be good at.

A photographer is embedded with the Paris unit that handles crimes against children, and her camera is the film's alibi for looking. Maïwenn builds Polisse out of that arrangement. Fred and his colleagues in the BPM work cases involving offenses against the weakest people in the city, and they have to endure being watched while they do it by Melissa, commissioned to document the team's routine. A hundred and twenty-three minutes is long enough for procedure to turn into habit, which is the point — the unit's habits are load-bearing, and the film keeps leaning on them to see what gives. It has drawn academic attention for the way its people switch languages, Arabic among them, to take or cede ground inside a room. That is a precise thing to notice about a film whose surface sounds like noise.

A family sets about the long, unheroic work of helping an eight-year-old recover from something done to her. So-won survived it; that is where Lee Joon-ik starts, and the two hours that follow belong to the household around her, to parents who have to be steady in front of the child and then find somewhere to put a rage they cannot show her. The pressure is double, and it runs in one house on the same days. Recovery has no plot shape: it is repetition, appointments, patience, adult feeling managed in a room where a child is listening. A hundred and twenty-two minutes is a long time to spend with people who are being careful. The length is the argument: careful is not a mood here, it is labor, and it has to be done again tomorrow.
